# Quantum-group symmetry on the half-line {#sec-boundary-qg}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false title="Learning goals"}
- See how a boundary breaks the non-local charges of Part VI, and which combinations survive.
- Understand why the surviving charges form a coideal subalgebra, not a Hopf subalgebra, of $U_q(\hat g)$.
- Derive soliton reflection matrices from linear intertwining equations, and prove that they solve the reflection equation.
- Rederive the Ghoshal–Zamolodchikov sine-Gordon reflection matrix from eight linear equations.
- Relate the quantum boundary parameters $\hat\epsilon_j$ to the classical $C_j$, and see why first-order perturbation theory around Neumann cannot fix them.
:::

In the bulk, the S-matrix was found in two steps (@sec-qg-symmetry): the non-local charges of Bernard and LeClair generate $U_q(\hat g^\vee)$, and the S-matrix is an intertwiner of this symmetry, so it is $\Phi\check R$ with $\check R$ obtained by solving linear equations. This chapter does the same on the half-line. The boundary breaks half of the bulk symmetry. What survives is a subalgebra $B\subset U_q(\hat g)$, generated by one combination $b_j$ of $e_j$, $f_j$ and $k_j$ for each node, and the reflection matrix is an intertwiner of $B$.

The subalgebra $B$ is not a Hopf algebra. It is a *coideal*: its coproduct lands in $U_q(\hat g)\otimes B$. This is exactly what is needed to act on multi-soliton states in front of a boundary, and exactly what is needed to prove that every intertwiner solves the reflection equation of @sec-reflection-equation. The construction is due to Delius and MacKay [@delius_mackay2003], building on the charges that Mezincescu and Nepomechie found for boundary sine-Gordon [@mezincescu_nepomechie1998]. We redo it in the conventions of Part VI. Several statements of the original need correcting, and we flag them as we go. @sec-soliton-reflection applies the method to the soliton multiplets, and @sec-qsp places the coideals in the mathematical theory of quantum symmetric pairs.

## Boundary conformal perturbation theory {#sec-boundary-cpt}

We need just enough of boundary conformal perturbation theory to see which charges survive. As in @sec-nonlocal-charges, view the imaginary-coupling theory as a free massless boson perturbed by the potential $V_{\rm imag}$. On the whole line the free field splits into chiral halves, $\vec\phi=\vec\varphi(x^+)+\bar{\vec\varphi}(x^-)$, and the non-local currents are chiral vertex operators.

**Neumann boundary as parity images.** The free boson on $x\le0$ with Neumann boundary condition $\partial_x\vec\phi|_{x=0}=0$ is described by the parity-even fields of the theory on the whole line. To every field $\Phi(x,t)$ on the line there corresponds a field on the half-line,

$$
\tilde\Phi(x,t)=\Phi(x,t)+\bar\Phi(-x,t),\qquad x\le0 ,
$$ {#eq-parity-image}

where $\bar\Phi$ is the parity transform of $\Phi$. In particular $\tilde\phi(x,t)=\phi(x,t)+\phi(-x,t)$ satisfies the Neumann condition, and its chiral components are $\tilde\varphi(x,t)=\varphi(x,t)+\bar\varphi(-x,t)$ and $\tilde{\bar\varphi}(x,t)=\bar\varphi(x,t)+\varphi(-x,t)$. The new feature is that the holomorphic and antiholomorphic halves now have a non-zero two-point function, because each contains the image of the other. The bulk perturbation is parity invariant, so it is also a valid perturbation of the Neumann theory. So $\phi$ is the free field on the whole line, $\tilde\phi$ is the free field on the half-line, and on $x\le0$ the latter is the parity-even combination of the former and its image. The bulk perturbation of the half-line theory is $\int d^2x\,V(\phi)$ written with the whole-line field, which is parity invariant and so acts within the parity-even sector. Delius and MacKay stress that perturbing by $\int d^2x\,V(\tilde\phi)$ instead would not give the affine Toda theory on the half-line [@delius_mackay2003, sec. 3.2]: since $\tilde\phi$ contains the image field, $V(\tilde\phi)$ is a different operator.

**Boundary perturbation.** A general integrable boundary is reached by adding a boundary term, a sum of boundary vertex operators $\sum_j\epsilon_j\,e^{i\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\tilde\phi(0,t)/2}$, which is the quantum version of the boundary potential $\mathcal B_{\rm imag}$ of @sec-boundary-potential with $\epsilon_j\propto C_j$. To first order in the boundary coupling $\lambda_b$, the boundary condition follows from the operator product of $\partial_x\tilde\phi(x,t)$ with the boundary perturbation at $t'$. The two image terms give simple poles $(t-t'+ix)^{-1}$ and $(t-t'-ix)^{-1}$ with opposite signs, and the identity

$$
\lim_{x\to0^-}\left[\frac1{(t-t'+ix)^n}-\frac1{(t-t'-ix)^n}\right]=\frac{2\pi i}{(n-1)!}\,\partial_{t'}^{\,n-1}\delta(t-t')
$$ {#eq-image-delta}

turns the difference into a contact term at the boundary. For $n=1$ this reproduces the classical boundary condition $\partial_x\vec\phi|_0=-\nabla\mathcal B$ at first order [@delius_mackay2003, sec. 3.3]. For $n=2$ it gives a total time derivative, which is what we need next.

## Non-local charges on the half-line {#sec-boundary-charges}

**Parity and the Neumann charges.** Parity maps $x\to-x$ and exchanges left- and right-movers. It therefore exchanges the charges built from $\vec\varphi$ with those built from $\bar{\vec\varphi}$, and reverses the topological charge:

$$
P:\quad Q_j\leftrightarrow\bar Q_j,\qquad T_j\mapsto-T_j .
$$

For sine-Gordon, with the labels of @sec-qg-coproduct, this reads $Q_\pm\leftrightarrow\bar Q_\mp$. The combinations $\tilde Q_j=Q_j+\bar Q_j$ are parity even, and can be written as integrals over $x\le0$ of the image currents (-@eq-parity-image). Their time derivative is a boundary term, the difference of the holomorphic current and its image at $x=0$. For the Neumann boundary of the free theory the two coincide, so $\tilde Q_j$ is conserved. The topological charges $T_j$ are not conserved on the half-line: the boundary can absorb topological charge. But $q^{T_j}$ survives in a different role. On the half-line $T_j=\frac\beta{2\pi}\vec\alpha_j\cdot\big(\vec\phi(0,t)-\vec\phi(-\infty,t)\big)$, so $q^{T_j}$ is a boundary vertex operator.

**The boundary term.** With the boundary perturbation switched on, the time derivative of $\tilde Q_j$ is computed at first order from the operator product of the image currents with the boundary vertex operators. The relevant singularity is a double pole, so (-@eq-image-delta) with $n=2$ produces a total time derivative of the boundary operator $e^{i(\cdots)\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi(0,t)}$. The exponent is exactly the one of $q^{T_j}$ [@delius_mackay2003, eqs. (3.25)–(3.28) and (4.10)]:

$$
\partial_t\big(Q_j+\bar Q_j\big)=-\hat\epsilon_j\,\partial_tq^{T_j}+O(\lambda_b^2),\qquad \hat\epsilon_j\propto\lambda_b\,\epsilon_j .
$$

The conserved charges are therefore

$$
\hat Q_j=Q_j+\bar Q_j+\hat\epsilon_j\,q^{T_j},\qquad j=0,\dots,r .
$$ {#eq-boundary-charges}

Mezincescu and Nepomechie had found these charges for boundary sine-Gordon at the free-fermion point by direct computation [@mezincescu_nepomechie1998]. In $\hat\epsilon_j\propto\lambda_b\epsilon_j$ the label $j$ is that of Delius and MacKay's $a_n$ computation, in which the charge of node $j$ meets the boundary term of the same node [@delius_mackay2003, eqs. (4.8)–(4.12)]. For sine-Gordon the labels of @sec-qg-coproduct also pair each node with itself, but @cnj-bsg-uv-ir pairs them crossed, $\hat\epsilon_1$ with $C_0$ and $\hat\epsilon_0$ with $C_1$; the two differ by charge conjugation (@sec-bsg-parameters). We return in @sec-epsilon-constraint to what the first-order computation does and does not determine.

**Book conventions.** The dictionary of @sec-qg-coproduct identifies $Q_j\to e_j$, $q^{T_j}\to k_j$, and $\bar Q_jq^{-T_j}\to f_j$ up to a constant. So $\bar Q_j\propto f_jk_j$, and the conserved charges are

$$
b_j=e_j+q_j^{-1}f_jk_j+\hat\epsilon_j\,k_j,\qquad q_j^{-1}f_jk_j=k_j^{1/2}f_jk_j^{1/2},\qquad j=0,\dots,r .
$$ {#eq-coideal-generators}

The coefficient of $f_jk_j$ is not a convention. Rescaling $e_j\to s_je_j$, $f_j\to f_j/s_j$ is an automorphism of $U_q(\hat g)$. It maps the generator with coefficient $c_j$ to one with coefficient $c_j/s_j^2$, and $\hat\epsilon_j$ to $\hat\epsilon_j/s_j$, so only $\hat\epsilon_j^2/c_j$ is invariant under it. The value $c_j=q_j^{-1}$ comes from the normalization of the charges. Parity exchanges $Q_j$ and $\bar Q_j$, and Delius and MacKay normalize both with the same constant, so the two terms of $Q_j+\bar Q_j$ come with relative coefficient 1. With $Q_j=e_j$ and $\bar Q_j=c_jf_jk_j$, the relations of @sec-qg-coproduct give $Q_j\bar Q_j-q_j^{-2}\bar Q_jQ_j=c_j(k_j^2-1)/(q_j-q_j^{-1})$. Their (4.26), corrected by $T_j\to T_j/2$ (@sec-boundary-qg-notes) and translated by the dictionary, has the right-hand side $(k_j^2-1)/(q_j^2-1)$, so $c_j=q_j^{-1}$ [@delius_mackay2003, eq. (4.26)]. The expansion of the $\mathcal B$-matrix in @sec-reflection-algebra returns exactly this coefficient. Independently, for sine-Gordon a reflection matrix exists only if $c_0c_1=q^{-2}$ (@sec-sg-k-from-symmetry), and $c_0=c_1=q^{-1}$ is the symmetric solution of this condition. The values of $\hat\epsilon_j$ quoted in this part all refer to $c_j=q_j^{-1}$.

## Coideal subalgebras {#sec-coideal}

Let $B_{\hat\epsilon}\subset U_q(\hat g)$ be the subalgebra generated by the $b_j$ of (-@eq-coideal-generators). With the Part VI coproduct $\Delta(e_j)=e_j\otimes1+k_j\otimes e_j$, $\Delta(f_j)=f_j\otimes k_j^{-1}+1\otimes f_j$:

::: {#prp-coideal-left}
## Left coideal
**[Established]** [@delius_mackay2003]

$$
\Delta(b_j)=\big(e_j+q_j^{-1}f_jk_j\big)\otimes1+k_j\otimes b_j=(b_j-\hat\epsilon_jk_j)\otimes1+k_j\otimes b_j\ \in\ U_q(\hat g)\otimes B_{\hat\epsilon} .
$$ {#eq-coideal-coproduct}

So $B_{\hat\epsilon}$ is a left coideal subalgebra: $\Delta(B_{\hat\epsilon})\subset U_q(\hat g)\otimes B_{\hat\epsilon}$. It is not a Hopf subalgebra: that would need $k_j\otimes b_j\in B_{\hat\epsilon}\otimes B_{\hat\epsilon}$, so $k_j\in B_{\hat\epsilon}$, which the intersection property of @sec-letzter-kolb excludes for the quantum symmetric pair coideals. The Hopf subalgebra generated by $e_j$ and $k_j$ is not conserved.
:::

::: {.proof}
$\Delta(f_jk_j)=(f_j\otimes k_j^{-1}+1\otimes f_j)(k_j\otimes k_j)=f_jk_j\otimes1+k_j\otimes f_jk_j$ and $\Delta(k_j)=k_j\otimes k_j$. Add $\Delta(e_j)$. The terms with $k_j$ in the first factor combine into $k_j\otimes b_j$. Checked on tensor products of spin-$j$ and $a_n$ representations in `code/boundary_coideal.py`.
:::

**Why a coideal.** Consider $N$ solitons in front of the boundary, which sits at the right end. The state space is $V_1(\theta_1)\otimes\dots\otimes V_N(\theta_N)$, ordered from left to right, and a charge acts on it by the iterated coproduct. In the bulk, the coproduct records that the charge density at $x$ sees the topological charge of everything to its left (@sec-qg-coproduct). On the half-line nothing changes for the solitons far from the boundary, which see the full $U_q(\hat g)$. Only the last tensor factor is in contact with the boundary, and only there must the action be restricted to $B$. The iterated coproduct of a left coideal lies in $U_q(\hat g)^{\otimes(N-1)}\otimes B$, which is exactly this structure. A Hopf subalgebra would be too small: neither $e_j$ nor $f_j$ is conserved on its own. The boundary itself, or a boundary bound state, is one more tensor factor on the right that carries a representation of $B$ only.

**Classical limit.** As $q\to1$, $b_j\to e_j+f_j+\hat\epsilon_j$. The elements $e_j+f_j$ are fixed by the Chevalley involution $e_j\leftrightarrow f_j$, so $B_0$ is a quantization of the fixed-point subalgebra of an involution. This is the root of the connection with quantum symmetric pairs (@sec-letzter-kolb). The special values $\hat\epsilon_j=\pm\epsilon_*$ of @prp-an-k-existence have no such limit, because $\epsilon_*$ diverges as $q\to1$ (@sec-symmetric-pairs).

## Reflection matrices as intertwiners {#sec-k-intertwiner}

A soliton of multiplet $\mu$ with rapidity $\theta$ hits the boundary and returns with rapidity $-\theta$. If the boundary conjugates solitons, it returns in the conjugate multiplet $\bar\mu$ (the boundaries of @sec-durham-classification). If it preserves them, it returns in $\mu$ (@sec-soliton-preserving). Since the $b_j$ are conserved, the reflection matrix commutes with them:

$$
K_\mu(\theta)\,\pi_{\mu,\theta}(b_j)=\pi_{\bar\mu,-\theta}(b_j)\,K_\mu(\theta)\qquad\text{for all }j .
$$ {#eq-k-intertwiner}

With $y=y(\theta)$ the principal-gradation variable of @sec-amplitude-and-gradation, $\pi_{\mu,-\theta}$ is the representation at $1/y$. The equation is linear in $K$. It is the boundary analogue of Jimbo's equations (-@eq-jimbo), and like them it is much easier to solve than the reflection equation.

::: {#thm-k-reflection}
## Intertwiners solve the reflection equation
**[Theorem]** Suppose that (i) $K_\mu$ and $K_\nu$ satisfy (-@eq-k-intertwiner) for the same $B_{\hat\epsilon}$; (ii) for generic $\theta_1,\theta_2$ the only $B_{\hat\epsilon}$-endomorphisms of $V_\mu(\theta_1)\otimes V_\nu(\theta_2)$ and of $V_{\bar\mu}(-\theta_1)\otimes V_{\bar\nu}(-\theta_2)$, with $B_{\hat\epsilon}$ acting by the coproduct, are scalars (checked numerically for $a_1,a_2,a_3$ in `code/boundary_coideal.py`); and (iii) the R-matrices are normalized so that both sides agree at one point, for example on highest weights. Then, with $x_i=x(\theta_i)$,

$$
\check R_{\bar\nu\bar\mu}\Big(\frac{x_1}{x_2}\Big)K^\mu_2(x_1)\,\check R_{\mu\bar\nu}(x_1x_2)\,K^\nu_2(x_2)=K^\nu_2(x_2)\,\check R_{\nu\bar\mu}(x_1x_2)\,K^\mu_2(x_1)\,\check R_{\mu\nu}\Big(\frac{x_1}{x_2}\Big),
$$

the soliton-conjugating reflection equation of @sec-reflection-equation, with $K_2=1\otimes K$. For a soliton-preserving boundary drop the bars, which gives the braid form with a single R-matrix when $\mu=\nu$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Both sides map $V_\mu(\theta_1)\otimes V_\nu(\theta_2)$ to $V_{\bar\mu}(-\theta_1)\otimes V_{\bar\nu}(-\theta_2)$. Each factor commutes with the action of $B$. For $\check R$ this holds because it intertwines $\Delta(a)$ for every $a\in U_q(\hat g)$. For $1\otimes K$ it follows from (-@eq-coideal-coproduct): the term $(b_j-\hat\epsilon_jk_j)\otimes1$ commutes with $1\otimes K$ trivially, and $(k_j\otimes b_j)(1\otimes K)=k_j\otimes b_jK=(1\otimes K)(k_j\otimes b_j)$ by (-@eq-k-intertwiner). Here the coideal property is essential: the second tensor factor only ever sees elements of $B$. So both sides are $B$-intertwiners from $V_\mu(\theta_1)\otimes V_\nu(\theta_2)$ to $V_{\bar\mu}(-\theta_1)\otimes V_{\bar\nu}(-\theta_2)$. For generic $\theta_i$ every factor is invertible, so the right-hand side inverted times the left-hand side is a $B$-endomorphism of $V_\mu(\theta_1)\otimes V_\nu(\theta_2)$, and by (ii) it is a scalar. Hypothesis (iii) fixes the constant.
:::

Hypothesis (ii) is the real content. It is Schur's lemma in the form needed here, and it follows from irreducibility under $B$. $B$ is smaller than $U_q(\hat g)$, so (ii) is a stronger statement than irreducibility under $U_q(\hat g)$. If $B$ were too small, $K$ would not be unique and the argument would fail. If $B$ were too large, no intertwiner would exist. Delius and MacKay describe the required coideals as "small enough" for intertwiners to exist and "large enough" for tensor products to stay irreducible [@delius_mackay2003, sec. 5]. We have checked (ii) numerically for $a_2$ and $a_3$, for all four pairs $(\mu,\nu)\in\{V,\bar V\}^2$ at $\hat\epsilon=0$, $s=\pm1$ and generic $\hat\epsilon$, and for $a_1$ spin $\frac12\otimes\frac12$ and $\frac12\otimes1$ (`code/boundary_coideal.py`). At generic $\hat\epsilon$ the endomorphisms are still scalars but no $K$ exists, which is the case of a $B$ that is too large. A general proof, valid for every $\hat\epsilon$, follows from Appel and Vlaar's generic irreducibility theorem and is sketched in @prp-hypothesis-ii. It gives uniqueness, not existence. In every case in this part we verify the reflection equation numerically as well (`code/boundary_coideal.py`, `code/reflection_matrices.py`).

Hypothesis (iii) is a normalization, not a condition: rescaling one $\check R$ rescales one side only. What has content is the constant for the physical amplitudes, scalar factor times $\check R$. Charge conjugation and parity make the scalar factors on the two sides equal, $S^0_{\bar\nu\bar\mu}=S^0_{\nu\mu}=S^0_{\mu\nu}$ and $S^0_{\mu\bar\nu}=S^0_{\bar\nu\mu}=S^0_{\nu\bar\mu}$, so the constant is that of the matrix parts. With R-matrices normalized to 1 on highest weights, it is exactly 1 when $\mu=\nu$.

**Boundary bound states.** Solitons can bind to the boundary (@sec-boundary-bound-states). A multiplet of boundary bound states spans a space $V_{[\lambda]}$ that carries a representation of $B$, not of $U_q(\hat g)$, since it is a tensor factor at the right end. The reflection of a soliton off such a state is an intertwiner of $(\pi_\mu\otimes\pi_{[\lambda]})\Delta(b_j)$:

$$
K_{\mu[\lambda]}(\theta):V_\mu(\theta)\otimes V_{[\lambda]}\to V_{\bar\mu}(-\theta)\otimes V_{[\lambda]} .
$$

The boundary ground state is the simplest case. Since $Q_j$ and $\bar Q_j$ annihilate it and $T_j=0$, it is the one-dimensional $B$-module $b_j\mapsto\hat\epsilon_j$, and (-@eq-coideal-coproduct) gives back (-@eq-k-intertwiner).

::: {#prp-boundary-module}
## One-dimensional boundary modules
**[Proposition, sketch]** Let $V_{[\lambda]}$ be a one-dimensional $B$-module, $b_j\mapsto\beta_j$. On $V_\mu\otimes V_{[\lambda]}$ the coproduct acts as $e_j+q_j^{-1}f_jk_j+\beta_jk_j$ on the first factor. So the reflection matrix off this boundary state is the ground-state reflection matrix with $\hat\epsilon_j$ replaced by $\beta_j$.
:::

::: {.proof}
$(\pi_\mu\otimes\pi_{[\lambda]})\Delta(b_j)=\pi_\mu(b_j-\hat\epsilon_jk_j)+\beta_j\pi_\mu(k_j)$ by (-@eq-coideal-coproduct).
:::

In boundary sine-Gordon every boundary bound state is a singlet, and Bajnok, Palla, Takács and Tóth found that its reflection matrix has the Ghoshal–Zamolodchikov form with shifted parameters [@bptt2002]. The proposition explains why the matrix structure is the same, and the $\beta_j$ can be found from the representation theory of $B$. At the reflected rapidities $y=e^{-i\lambda\nu_n}$ of the bound-state poles $\theta=i\nu_n$ (@sec-bsg-spectrum), $V(y)\otimes\mathbb C_{\hat\epsilon}$ has a one-dimensional $B$-submodule, with $\beta_{1,0}=-\cos(\bar\eta\pm i\vartheta)/\sin\pi\lambda$ and $\bar\eta=\pi(\lambda+1)-\eta$, the same for all $n$. By the proposition this is exactly the matrix part of the excited-state reflection matrix (-@eq-bsg-excited-k) [@bptt2002]: (-@eq-bsg-eta-theta) with $\eta\to\bar\eta$ and $\vartheta\to-\vartheta$, which exchanges $s$ and $\bar s$. The states $|n\rangle$ differ only in their CDD factors $a_n$ (checked numerically for $n=0,1,2$ in `code/boundary_coideal.py`). In $a_n^{(1)}$ the boundary bound states can form non-trivial multiplets [@delius_mackay2003, sec. 4.2], and their reflection matrices need the representation theory of $B$ (@sec-qsp). The possible values of the $\beta_j$ for $a_n^{(1)}$ and $d_n^{(1)}$ are listed in @prp-one-dim-modules.

## Worked example: sine-Gordon {#sec-sg-k-from-symmetry}

Take the soliton doublet $V(y)$ with basis $(s,\bar s)$, $y=e^{\lambda\theta}$ and the physical $q=-e^{-i\pi\lambda}$ (@sec-qg-coproduct). In the principal gradation of @sec-amplitude-and-gradation, $e_1=yE$, $f_1=F/y$, $k_1=q^H=\mathrm{diag}(q,q^{-1})$, $e_0=yF$, $f_0=E/y$, $k_0=q^{-H}$, with $H=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1)$ (we write $q^H$ for the Cartan generator $K$ of @sec-uqsl2, to keep $K$ for reflection matrices). Then $q^{-1}Fq^H=F$ and $q^{-1}Eq^{-H}=E$, and the generators (-@eq-coideal-generators) are

$$
\pi_y(b_1)=\begin{pmatrix}\hat\epsilon_1q&y\\y^{-1}&\hat\epsilon_1q^{-1}\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\pi_y(b_0)=\begin{pmatrix}\hat\epsilon_0q^{-1}&y^{-1}\\y&\hat\epsilon_0q\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-sg-coideal-rep}

Since $V\cong\bar V$ for $a_1^{(1)}$, the reflection matrix maps $V(y)$ to $V(1/y)$. The intertwining equation $K\pi_y(b_j)=\pi_{1/y}(b_j)K$ for $j=0,1$ is a set of eight homogeneous linear equations for the four entries of $K$.

::: {#prp-sg-k-unique}
## The sine-Gordon reflection matrix
**[Theorem]** (i) With general coefficients $c_j$ in place of $q^{-1}$ and $\hat\epsilon=0$, a non-zero solution exists if and only if $c_0c_1=q^{-2}$. (ii) For $c_0=c_1=q^{-1}$ and any $\hat\epsilon_0,\hat\epsilon_1$ the solution is unique up to a factor:

$$
K(\theta)\propto\begin{pmatrix}(q-q^{-1})(\hat\epsilon_1y+\hat\epsilon_0y^{-1})&y^2-y^{-2}\\ y^2-y^{-2}&(q-q^{-1})(\hat\epsilon_0y+\hat\epsilon_1y^{-1})\end{pmatrix},\qquad y=e^{\lambda\theta} .
$$ {#eq-sg-k-coideal}
:::

::: {.proof}
(ii) Write $K=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$. The diagonal entries of both equations give $b=c$. The $(1,2)$ entries give

$$
ay-dy^{-1}=\hat\epsilon_1(q-q^{-1})\,b,\qquad ay^{-1}-dy=-\hat\epsilon_0(q-q^{-1})\,b ,
$$

and the $(2,1)$ entries repeat them. Eliminating $d$ and $a$ in turn gives $a(y^2-y^{-2})=(q-q^{-1})(\hat\epsilon_1y+\hat\epsilon_0y^{-1})b$ and $d(y^2-y^{-2})=(q-q^{-1})(\hat\epsilon_0y+\hat\epsilon_1y^{-1})b$. (i) is a rank computation, done symbolically in `code/boundary_coideal.py`, which also checks (ii).
:::

This is the matrix of Ghoshal and Zamolodchikov [@gz1994]. With $\hat\epsilon_1=\varepsilon e^{i\xi_B}$, $\hat\epsilon_0=\varepsilon e^{-i\xi_B}$ and $k=1/(\varepsilon\sin\pi\lambda)$, and $u=-i\theta$, it becomes their form $\cos(\xi_B+\lambda u)$, $\cos(\xi_B-\lambda u)$ on the diagonal and $\frac k2\sin2\lambda u$ off it (@sec-bsg-k-matrix). We write $\xi_B$ for their boundary parameter, to avoid a clash with $\xi=\pi/\lambda$ of @sec-sine-gordon. Three special points are worth knowing.

**Neumann.** Ghoshal and Zamolodchikov's free boundary condition has $\xi_B=0$ and $k=1/\sin(\pi\lambda/2)$. In coideal language it is

$$
\hat\epsilon_0=\hat\epsilon_1=\epsilon_*\equiv\frac1{\sqrt{(1-q)(1-q^{-1})}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2-q-q^{-1}}}=\frac1{2\cos(\pi\lambda/2)} .
$$ {#eq-sg-neumann-eps}

The same point is $(\eta,\vartheta)=(\frac\pi2(\lambda+1),0)$ in the parametrization of Bajnok, Palla, Takács and Tóth [@bptt2002] (@sec-bsg-parameters).

**$\hat\epsilon=0$.** $K$ is purely off-diagonal: every soliton reflects into an antisoliton. This is $(\eta,\vartheta)=(\frac\pi2,0)$. It is not Neumann.

**Dirichlet.** $\vartheta\to\infty$, so $\hat\epsilon_j\to\infty$ and $K$ becomes diagonal (unchecked).

The numerical checks of these identifications, of boundary unitarity and of crossing-unitarity are in `code/boundary_sine_gordon.py`.

**The sign of $q$.** Replacing $q$ by $-q$ maps $K(\hat\epsilon;-q)$ to $K(-\hat\epsilon;q)$, up to a diagonal gauge, and the reflection equation is invariant. So the reflection equation cannot detect the sign of $q$. Boundary crossing-unitarity can. With plain conjugation $s\leftrightarrow\bar s$ it holds only at the physical $q=-e^{-i\pi\lambda}$, exactly as the bulk crossing test of @sec-crossing-sign. At $-q$ it needs the twisted conjugation matrix of that section.

## The reflection-equation algebra {#sec-reflection-algebra}

The charges (-@eq-boundary-charges) were found at first order in perturbation theory. Could higher orders add terms that are invisible in the vector representation? Delius and MacKay answer this with a construction that needs no perturbation theory, only one known solution of the reflection equation [@delius_mackay2003, sec. 2.3]. It is an affine, quantum version of Sklyanin's construction of the double-row monodromy matrix [@sklyanin1988].

Let $\mathcal R$ be the universal R-matrix of $U_q(\hat g)$ with the Part VI coproduct. Because this coproduct is the opposite of that of @sec-hopf, $\mathcal R$ is the flip of the universal R-matrix of @sec-universal-r. It still satisfies (-@eq-universal-r-intertwines) and (-@eq-quasitriangular). Given a reflection matrix $K_\mu(\theta):V_\mu(\theta)\to V_{\bar\mu}(-\theta)$, define the $U_q(\hat g)$-valued matrices

$$
L^\mu_\theta=(\pi_{\mu,\theta}\otimes1)(\mathcal R),\qquad \bar L^{\bar\mu}_\theta=(\pi_{\bar\mu,-\theta}\otimes1)(\mathcal R^{\rm op}),\qquad
\mathcal B^\mu_\theta=\bar L^{\bar\mu}_\theta\,(K_\mu(\theta)\otimes1)\,L^\mu_\theta .
$$ {#eq-b-matrix}

In components, $(\mathcal B^\mu_\theta)^\alpha{}_\beta=(\bar L^{\bar\mu}_\theta)^\alpha{}_\gamma K_\mu(\theta)^\gamma{}_\delta(L^\mu_\theta)^\delta{}_\beta\in U_q(\hat g)$.

::: {#prp-b-coideal}
## The B-matrix generates a coideal
**[Established]** [@delius_mackay2003] (i) The entries of $\mathcal B^\mu_\theta$, for all $\theta$, generate a left coideal subalgebra:

$$
\Delta\big((\mathcal B^\mu_\theta)^\alpha{}_\beta\big)=(\bar L^{\bar\mu}_\theta)^\alpha{}_\delta(L^\mu_\theta)^\sigma{}_\beta\otimes(\mathcal B^\mu_\theta)^\delta{}_\sigma .
$$ {#eq-b-coproduct}

(ii) A matrix $K_\nu(\theta')$ commutes with all the entries of $\mathcal B^\mu_\theta$, in the sense of (-@eq-k-intertwiner), if and only if $K_\mu$ and $K_\nu$ satisfy the reflection equation.
:::

::: {.proof}
(i) The second identity of (-@eq-quasitriangular), $(1\otimes\Delta)\mathcal R=\mathcal R_{13}\mathcal R_{12}$, evaluated in $V_\mu$ on the first factor, gives $\Delta(L^\alpha{}_\beta)=L^\gamma{}_\beta\otimes L^\alpha{}_\gamma$. The first identity, flipped, gives $(1\otimes\Delta)\mathcal R^{\rm op}=\mathcal R^{\rm op}_{12}\mathcal R^{\rm op}_{13}$, so $\Delta(\bar L^\alpha{}_\beta)=\bar L^\alpha{}_\gamma\otimes\bar L^\gamma{}_\beta$. Hence

$$
\Delta(\mathcal B^\alpha{}_\beta)=\big(\bar L^\alpha{}_\epsilon\otimes\bar L^\epsilon{}_\gamma\big)K^\gamma{}_\delta\big(L^\sigma{}_\beta\otimes L^\delta{}_\sigma\big)=\bar L^\alpha{}_\epsilon L^\sigma{}_\beta\otimes\bar L^\epsilon{}_\gamma K^\gamma{}_\delta L^\delta{}_\sigma ,
$$

which is (-@eq-b-coproduct). (ii) Evaluate the second factor of (-@eq-b-matrix) in $V_\nu(\theta')$. Then $L^\mu_\theta$ becomes the R-matrix on $V_\mu(\theta)\otimes V_\nu(\theta')$, $\bar L^{\bar\mu}_\theta$ the R-matrix on $V_\nu(\theta')\otimes V_{\bar\mu}(-\theta)$ conjugated by the flip, and the same in $V_{\bar\nu}(-\theta')$. The commutation of $1\otimes K_\nu(\theta')$ with $(1\otimes\pi)(\mathcal B^\mu_\theta)$ becomes, after using $P\check R\propto S$, exactly the reflection equation of @thm-k-reflection [@delius_mackay2003, eqs. (2.14)–(2.20)].
:::

The $\mathcal B$-matrices satisfy the quadratic relations obtained from the reflection equation by replacing $K$ with $\mathcal B$. Algebras defined by such relations are Sklyanin's reflection-equation algebras [@sklyanin1988], whose general algebraic structure was described by Kulish and Sklyanin [@kulish_sklyanin1992]. So (-@eq-b-matrix) embeds a reflection-equation algebra into $U_q(\hat g)$ as a coideal. For the $a_n^{(1)}$ vector representation Delius and MacKay expand $\mathcal B^\mu_\theta$ to first order in the spectral parameter. The coefficients of the off-diagonal elementary matrices are exactly the $\hat Q_j$ of (-@eq-boundary-charges) [@delius_mackay2003, eq. (4.35)]. In book conventions the universal R-matrix is $\mathcal R=q^{t}\big(1+\sum_j(q_j-q_j^{-1})f_j\otimes e_j+\dots\big)$, where $q^t$ acts on a product of weight vectors of weights $\lambda,\mu$ as $q^{(\lambda,\mu)}$ (for $sl_2$, $q^{t}=q^{\frac12H\otimes H}$). Since $f_j$ carries $y^{-1}$ in the principal gradation, $\mathcal B^\mu_\theta$ is expanded in $1/y$. For the $a_n$ vector representation, with $K=1$ or (-@eq-an-k-matrix),

$$
\mathcal B=\kappa\Big[1+(q-q^{-1})\,y^{-1}\sum_j\pi_V(f_j)|_{y=1}\otimes b_j+O(y^{-2})\Big],
$$

with exactly the $b_j$ of (-@eq-coideal-generators), with $\hat\epsilon=0$ for $K=1$ and $\hat\epsilon=(s\epsilon_*,\epsilon_*,\dots,\epsilon_*)$ for (-@eq-an-k-matrix). This is checked for $n\le6$ in `code/boundary_coideal.py`, together with the leading terms of $\mathcal R$ against the exact $\check R$. It confirms that the perturbative charges are exact, with no higher-order corrections, and it confirms the coefficient $q_j^{-1}$ of $f_jk_j$ and the values of $\hat\epsilon_j$.

## Quantum and classical boundary parameters {#sec-epsilon-constraint}

For sine-Gordon, (-@eq-sg-k-coideal) exists for every $(\hat\epsilon_0,\hat\epsilon_1)$, matching the two-parameter family of classical boundary conditions ($C_0,C_1$ arbitrary in @sec-durham-classification). For $a_n^{(1)}$ with $n\ge2$ this is no longer so. The vector representation is the subject of @sec-an-nondiagonal-k, but the result is short.

::: {#prp-an-k-existence}
## Allowed quantum boundary parameters for $a_n^{(1)}$
**[Numerical]** for $n\le7$; **[Proposition, sketch]** in general. A reflection matrix $K:V(\theta)\to\bar V(-\theta)$ for the vector solitons exists, and is then unique, if and only if either all $\hat\epsilon_j=0$, when $K=1$, or

$$
\hat\epsilon_j^2=\epsilon_*^2=\frac1{(1-q)(1-q^{-1})}=\frac1{4\cos^2(\pi\omega/2)}\qquad\text{for all }j=0,\dots,n .
$$ {#eq-an-eps-condition}

Here $q=-e^{-i\pi\omega}$ with $\omega=\frac{4\pi}{\beta^2}-1$, the coupling of Part VI, which is $\lambda$ for sine-Gordon (@sec-bsg-k-matrix).

Sign patterns with the same $s=\prod_j\hat\epsilon_j/\epsilon_*$ are related by a diagonal gauge transformation. So the gauge-invariant data are a discrete sign $s=\pm1$, not a phase.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let node $j$ have $\alpha_j=\varepsilon_a-\varepsilon_b$. On $V(y)$ and $\bar V(1/y)$ the generator $b_j$ has the same off-diagonal part $A_j=y\,e_{ab}+y^{-1}e_{ba}$, and its diagonal parts are $\hat\epsilon_jk_j$ and $\hat\epsilon_jk_j^{-1}$. For a column $c\notin\{a,b\}$, the $(a,c)$ and $(b,c)$ entries of $KA_j+\hat\epsilon_jKk_j=A_jK+\hat\epsilon_jk_j^{-1}K$ involve only $K_{ac}$ and $K_{bc}$:

$$
\hat\epsilon_j(q^{-1}-1)K_{ac}+y\,K_{bc}=0,\qquad y^{-1}K_{ac}+\hat\epsilon_j(q-1)K_{bc}=0 ,
$$

with determinant $\hat\epsilon_j^2(1-q)(1-q^{-1})-1$. The same holds for the entries $(c,a)$, $(c,b)$ of a row $c\notin\{a,b\}$. These are the book's form of the corrected equations (4.19)–(4.20) of Delius and MacKay, and they are the origin of (-@eq-an-eps-condition). If $\hat\epsilon_j^2\ne\epsilon_*^2$ for every $j$, every off-diagonal entry of $K$ lies in such a pair of rows or columns, so $K$ is diagonal. The $(a,b)$ entries then give $K_{aa}=K_{bb}$, so $K\propto1$, which is their (4.18), and the $(a,a)$ entries give $\hat\epsilon_j(q^{-1}-q)K_{aa}=0$, so all $\hat\epsilon_j=0$. If all $\hat\epsilon_j^2=\epsilon_*^2$, the solution is (-@eq-an-k-matrix) and its gauge transforms (@sec-an-nondiagonal-k). Mixed patterns are excluded by propagating the vanishing entries from a node with $\hat\epsilon_j^2\ne\epsilon_*^2$ around the cycle of nodes; we have not written this step out in general.
:::

Checked for $n\le7$ in `code/boundary_coideal.py`, together with the $2\times2$ systems (symbolically for $a_3$). The script also shows that $|\hat\epsilon_j|=1$, random phases, and mixtures of zero and non-zero $\hat\epsilon_j$ all fail. The quantum parameter space is thus $\{0\}\cup\{\pm\epsilon_*\}^{n+1}$, discrete like the classical one, where all $C_j=0$ (Neumann) or all $C_j=\pm1$ [@bcdr1995]. Up to the gauge freedom on the quantum side and the coweight shifts of @sec-images-boundary on the classical side (which preserve $\prod_jC_j$ and connect all patterns with the same product), each side has three points: quantum $\hat\epsilon=0$, $s=+1$, $s=-1$; classical Neumann, $\prod_jC_j=+1$ (which contains $C\equiv+1$ and the solitonic patterns), $\prod_jC_j=-1$. The parallel is not a dictionary. @cnj-neumann-coideal below pairs $\hat\epsilon=0$ with the class of $C\equiv+1$ and $s=+1$ with Neumann, so $s$ does not correspond to $\prod_jC_j$. The quantum point $s=-1$ and the classical class $\prod_jC_j=-1$ are both left without a partner; whether they belong together is open (@sec-boundary-open-problems, problems 1 and 5). Baseilhac and Belliard had found (-@eq-an-eps-condition) earlier, for $a_n^{(1)}$, $d_n^{(1)}$ and $e_{6,7,8}^{(1)}$, as the condition under which the charges close on a generalized q-Onsager algebra [@baseilhac_belliard2010, Prop. 2.1]. Its algebraic origin is a Serre-type relation in $B$ (@prp-serre-obstruction).

Which quantum point is which boundary? Four pieces of evidence point the same way.

1. **Sine-Gordon, exactly.** The Neumann point (-@eq-sg-neumann-eps) is $\hat\epsilon_0=\hat\epsilon_1=\epsilon_*$, the $a_n$ special value at $n=1$, not $\hat\epsilon=0$.
2. **$a_2^{(1)}$, perturbatively.** Gandenberger found three solutions $K^+$, $K^-$, $K^d$ of the $a_2^{(1)}$ reflection equation [@gandenberger1999a]. They are our $s=+1$, $s=-1$ and $\hat\epsilon=0$ (@sec-an-nondiagonal-k). He showed that $K^+$ reproduces Kim's $O(\beta^2)$ Neumann reflection factor [@kim1995], while $K^d$ reproduces the $O(\beta^2)$ result for the uniform boundary $C\equiv+1$. On this basis he conjectured that $K^+$ belongs to the Neumann boundary [@gandenberger1999a, sec. 6].
3. **Semiclassics.** Delius and Gandenberger matched the diagonal solution to the classical time delays of the uniform boundary $C\equiv+1$ [@delius_gandenberger1999] (@sec-boundary-semiclassics).
4. **Duality, all $n$.** Delius and Gandenberger obtained the Neumann particle amplitudes by weak–strong duality from the amplitudes of the diagonal solution [@delius_gandenberger1999, eq. (3.20)], and found that they agree with Kim's $O(\beta^2)$ Neumann result for general $n$ [@delius_gandenberger1999, sec. 3.4]. This supports the assignment of $K=1$ to $C\equiv+1$ for all $n$; it does not test $s=+1$ directly.

::: {#cnj-neumann-coideal}
## Coideal parameters of the $a_n^{(1)}$ boundaries
**[Conjecture]** The Neumann boundary of $a_n^{(1)}$ affine Toda theory has $\hat\epsilon_j=\epsilon_*$ for all $j$ (the solution $s=+1$). The uniform boundary $C\equiv+1$ has $\hat\epsilon=0$ (the diagonal solution $K=1$).
:::

For $n=2$ the Neumann half of the conjecture is Gandenberger's [@gandenberger1999a, sec. 6]; @cnj-neumann-coideal extends it to all $n$. Its strongest support is that the $s=+1$ matrix, with its scalar factor, gives the Neumann particle amplitudes for $n=2,3,4$ and the classical Neumann time advance (@prp-an-nondiagonal-scalar, @sec-neumann-duality). The conjecture contradicts the reading of Delius and MacKay's first-order computation, in which the charges at the Neumann point are $Q_j+\bar Q_j$ and so $\hat\epsilon=0$ there. The resolution is the following.

::: {#prp-dm-first-order}
## What first-order perturbation theory fixes
**[Conjecture]** for $a_n$, $n\ge2$; for sine-Gordon it follows from @cnj-bsg-uv-ir. First-order boundary perturbation theory around the Neumann point determines $\partial\hat\epsilon_j/\partial\lambda_b$ at $\lambda_b=0$, not the value of $\hat\epsilon_j$ there: $\hat\epsilon_j=\epsilon_*+\kappa\,\lambda_b\epsilon_j+O(\lambda_b^2)$, with $\kappa$ the constant of [@delius_mackay2003, eq. (4.12)]. For sine-Gordon, (-@eq-bsg-eta-theta) and @cnj-bsg-uv-ir give exactly $\hat\epsilon_1=-\cos\big((\lambda+1)\arccos\mu_+\big)/\sin\pi\lambda$ and $\hat\epsilon_0=-\cos\big((\lambda+1)\arccos\mu_-\big)/\sin\pi\lambda$, with $\mu_\pm=(\tilde\mu/\tilde\mu_{\rm crit})e^{\pm i\beta_{\rm SG}\phi_0/2}$, so $\hat\epsilon_{1,0}=\epsilon_*-\frac{\lambda+1}{2\sin(\pi\lambda/2)}\mu_\pm+O(\mu^2)$. Since $\mu_+\propto C_0$ and $\mu_-\propto C_1$, node 1 is paired with $C_0$ and node 0 with $C_1$ (@sec-bsg-parameters).
:::

::: {.remark}
## Supporting argument
The computation of @sec-boundary-charges assumes that $Q_j+\bar Q_j$ is exactly conserved at $\lambda_b=0$. The argument for that used only the free-field boundary values $J_j(0)=\bar J_j(0)$ and $H_j(0)=\bar H_j(0)$. In Delius and MacKay's normalization the constant is $c=\sqrt{g\gamma^2(q_i^2-1)/2\pi i}\propto g^{1/2}$, where $g$ is the bulk coupling (their $\lambda$) [@delius_mackay2003, eq. (4.3)]. A term $\epsilon_*q^{T_j}$ in the normalized Neumann charge is therefore a term $\propto g^{1/2}$ in the unnormalized one, which has the same dimension as $\lambda_b$. Being non-analytic in the bulk coupling, it is invisible at every finite order of bulk perturbation theory, and the first-order computation in $\lambda_b$, done at $g=0$, cannot see it. That such a term is present is forced by the exact results: by (-@eq-sg-neumann-eps) for sine-Gordon, and by @prp-an-k-existence for $a_n$, where $\hat\epsilon_j$ cannot vary continuously away from $\{0,\pm\epsilon_*\}$ at all.
:::

For $a_n$ the boundary coupling cannot be switched on continuously from Neumann, so the perturbative statement is only formal there. What survives is its content for sine-Gordon, where the boundary parameters do vary continuously. There the exact map shows that each $\hat\epsilon$ depends on one boundary coupling $\mu_\pm$ only, and that $\hat\epsilon=0$ at $\phi_0=0$ lies at $\tilde\mu/\tilde\mu_{\rm crit}=\cos\frac\pi{2(\lambda+1)}$, which tends to the uniform boundary as $\beta_{\rm SG}\to0$ (see the consequences of @cnj-bsg-uv-ir; checked in `code/boundary_coideal.py`).

## Exercises {#sec-boundary-qg-exercises}

::: {#exr-coideal-coproduct}
Verify (-@eq-coideal-coproduct) from the Part VI coproduct. Show that $B'$, generated by $e_j+c_jf_jk_j+\hat\epsilon_jk_j$ with general $c_j$, is also a left coideal. Find the automorphism of $U_q(\hat g)$ that maps $B'$ to $B_{\hat\epsilon'}$ of (-@eq-coideal-generators), and show that $\hat\epsilon_j^2/c_j$ is invariant.
:::

::: {#exr-why-not-right}
Show that $\Delta(b_j)\notin B\otimes U_q(\hat g)$. Explain why, with the Part VI coproduct, the boundary must sit at the right end of the tensor product. Where would it sit with the coproduct of @sec-hopf?
:::

::: {#exr-sg-eight-equations}
Write out the eight linear equations $K\pi_y(b_j)=\pi_{1/y}(b_j)K$ with (-@eq-sg-coideal-rep), and solve them to obtain (-@eq-sg-k-coideal). Repeat with general $c_0,c_1$ and $\hat\epsilon=0$, and show that a solution exists only if $c_0c_1=q^{-2}$.
:::

::: {#exr-sg-neumann}
Show that at the physical $q=-e^{-i\pi\lambda}$, $(1-q)(1-q^{-1})=4\cos^2(\pi\lambda/2)$. Substitute $\hat\epsilon_0=\hat\epsilon_1=\epsilon_*$ into (-@eq-sg-k-coideal), and compare the ratio of diagonal to off-diagonal entries with Ghoshal and Zamolodchikov's free boundary, $\xi_B=0$, $k=1/\sin(\pi\lambda/2)$.
:::

::: {#exr-boundary-unitarity-k}
Show that (-@eq-sg-k-coideal) satisfies $K(\theta)K(-\theta)\propto1$. *Hint:* $K(-\theta)$ intertwines $\pi_{1/y}$ with $\pi_y$, so $K(-\theta)K(\theta)$ is a $B$-endomorphism of $V(y)$. You also need that for generic $y$ the only such endomorphisms are scalars: show that $\pi_y(b_0)$ and $\pi_y(b_1)$ then have no common eigenvector.
:::

::: {#exr-boundary-module}
Use @prp-boundary-module to show that a one-dimensional boundary module with $\beta_0=\beta_1=0$ gives a purely off-diagonal sine-Gordon reflection matrix. Why is a one-dimensional $B$-module consistent with any pair $(\beta_0,\beta_1)$, when a one-dimensional $U_q(\hat g)$-module is not?
:::

::: {#exr-b-matrix}
Derive $\Delta(L^\alpha{}_\beta)=L^\gamma{}_\beta\otimes L^\alpha{}_\gamma$ from (-@eq-quasitriangular). Then complete the proof of (-@eq-b-coproduct).
:::

## Notes and references {#sec-boundary-qg-notes}

Non-local charges on the half-line were first written down by Mezincescu and Nepomechie for boundary sine-Gordon at the free-fermion point [@mezincescu_nepomechie1998]. Delius and MacKay derived them for sine-Gordon and $a_n^{(1)}$ affine Toda theory from boundary conformal perturbation theory, identified them as generators of coideal subalgebras, showed how to obtain reflection matrices from the linear intertwining equations, and gave the $\mathcal B=\bar L KL$ construction [@delius_mackay2003]. The rational analogue, with twisted Yangians, is due to Delius, MacKay and Short [@dms2001]. Reviews of the quantum affine case are [@delius2002] and [@delius_george2003]. The reflection equation itself goes back to Cherednik [@cherednik1984] and Sklyanin [@sklyanin1988]. The coideals reappear in mathematics as quantum symmetric pairs (@sec-qsp).

The treatment here follows Delius and MacKay, translated to the conventions of Part VI. Their paper contains the following slips, which are corrected in the text.

- **The sign and power of $q$.** Their $q=e^{+4\pi^2i/\beta^2}$ (their (3.10)) is the inverse of the physical value (-@eq-q-physical) for the same coproduct. For sine-Gordon this only flips $\hat\epsilon\to-\hat\epsilon$. For $a_n$ it decides whether the antisoliton is $\bar V(y)$ or $\bar V(-y)$, and only the physical value gives a solution of the reflection equation (`code/boundary_coideal.py`).
- **The factor 2 in their section 4.** With $|\alpha|^2=1$, the relation $[T_i,Q_j]=\alpha_i\cdot\alpha_jQ_j$ is inconsistent with their representation (4.13); their (4.26) holds on (4.13) only with $T_i\to T_i/2$ (`code/boundary_coideal.py`).
- **Equations (4.19)–(4.20).** The coefficients $\hat\epsilon_iq$ and $\hat\epsilon_iq^{-1}$ should be $\hat\epsilon_i(q-1)$ and $\hat\epsilon_i(q^{-1}-1)$: their coefficients correspond to taking $q^{T_i}=q^{-1}e_{ii}+q\,e_{i+1,i+1}$, forgetting that $q^{T_i}$ is 1 on the other basis vectors. Each pair of rows or columns also gives two equations, not one, and their determinant $1-\hat\epsilon_i^2(1-q)(1-q^{-1})$ is the origin of (-@eq-an-eps-condition) (proof of @prp-an-k-existence; the $2\times2$ systems are checked symbolically for $a_3$ in `code/boundary_coideal.py`).
- **The constraint after (4.20).** "$|\hat\epsilon_i|=1$" should be (-@eq-an-eps-condition), and the residual freedom $\prod_i\hat\epsilon_i$ is a sign, not a phase (`code/boundary_coideal.py`: $|\hat\epsilon_j|=1$ gives no $K$).
- **"If all $\hat\epsilon_i=0$ then $K$ can be an arbitrary diagonal matrix."** This contradicts their (4.18), which forces $K\propto1$ (`code/boundary_coideal.py`). Other diagonal matrices solve the reflection equation but intertwine a rescaled coideal (@sec-an-nondiagonal-k).
- **Neumann and $\hat\epsilon=0$.** Their first-order computation implicitly identifies the Neumann boundary with $\hat\epsilon=0$. By @prp-dm-first-order and @cnj-neumann-coideal, the Neumann boundary is at $\hat\epsilon_j=\epsilon_*$, and the diagonal solution belongs to the uniform boundary $C\equiv+1$, as Delius and Gandenberger had assigned it [@delius_gandenberger1999].

Ghoshal and Zamolodchikov's boundary parameter $\xi$ is written $\xi_B$ here. In their (5.9) all four operators on the right-hand sides should carry rapidity $-\theta$, as in their (3.22).
